node.label: Kenneth Pomeranz
node.date_label: The Making of a Hinterland 1993 · The Great Divergence 2000 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A historian of China whose reciprocal comparisons of Eurasian core regions recast the divergence of European and Chinese economies. The Great Divergence (2000) takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as the reverse question and argues that 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path'. Coal, and land-intensive goods from New World colonies worked by enslaved people, relieved Europe's constraints of land and energy. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) traces the economic and ecological costs for inland North China when the late Qing and Republican state abandoned many hinterland areas.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Kenneth Pomeranz (b. 1958); The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society, and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993); The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000). Readings: Bianco's review (1996); Cooper's review (2000); Huang's critique and Pomeranz's reply (2002).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the argument of The Great Divergence as its introduction states it (pp. 3–27 read, with the contents, in a preview of the later Princeton edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Making of a Hinterland is checked at contents level and through Bianco's 1996 review, read in full; its text is unread. He is not presented as the originator of reciprocal comparison: he writes that the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong', takes the 'encompassing comparison' from Charles Tilly, and notes parallels with Sugihara Kaoru. Arguments from colonial extraction (Williams, Frank, Amin) precede his. His estimates are contested: Cooper (2000) notes 'plausible guesstimates', and Bianco (1996) judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development. Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for the 2000 argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of Eurasian cores, joined to connections in a polycentric world (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own statement of method, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). Comparisons between scattered core regions should be 'truly reciprocal' (p. 8), 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm' (p. 8). With Tilly's 'encompassing comparison', 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach', and before 1800 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). The introduction ends 'with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot' (p. 25). He places the book as 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”' while warning that it 'treats the world’s regions very unevenly' and that 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history”' (p. 25). A contribution, not a founding: the approach was 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7), and 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed' (p. 8); the encompassing comparison is Tilly's (p. 10, n. 14). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The evidence is about method, so the edge targets reciprocal_comparison_resources ('Pomeranz names Wong’s reciprocal comparison and Tilly’s encompassing comparison as resources'; works: The Great Divergence, 7–10), which the checked pages match exactly. regional_divergence is an economic strand, not a global one. comparison and eurasian_states are shared with Wong and describe comparative development generally; protoindustry_trade_limits concerns Mokyr's model (pp. 21–23) and belongs to the argument rather than the method.

proposed_edges.relationship: Coal and New World resources enabled divergence between comparably developed Eurasian cores (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: regional_divergence ('Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources') holds him alone and states exactly the checked argument. divergence_household_dispute and coal_constraints_dispute pair him with Huang and rest on the 2002 exchange, a later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ecological constraint as economic history: hydraulic decay and deforestation in North China (1993) and land and fuel constraints across Eurasia (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The Making of a Hinterland (1993), checked at contents level: its chapters include 'Ecological Crisis and the Logic of “Self-strengthening”' (pp. 120–152), 'Sold Down the River?' (pp. 153–211) and 'Dealing with Disaster' (pp. 212–266), with appendices on 'Agricultural Losses from Hydraulic Decay' and 'Extra Transport Costs Incurred Because of Hydraulic Decay in Huang-Yun'. The publisher's description says it 'traces social, economic, and ecological change in inland North China'. Bianco's 1996 review (pp. 242–245, read in full) states that environmental degradation 'se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243), and describes a population deprived of wood and burning straw, grass, roots and dung needed as fertiliser (p. 244). In The Great Divergence (2000) he says he writes 'much more' than Wong about 'environmental change' (p. 8, n. 13); chapter 5 offers 'a systematic comparison of ecological constraints in selected key areas of China and Europe' (p. 12); and shortages 'of fuel and building materials' and threats to soil fertility appear in all the densest cores (p. 20). Cooper (2000, read) calls it 'a neo-Malthusian, ecological approach that focuses on access to food and raw materials'. Bianco also judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development (p. 244). edge_267 stays: it is an undirected comparison of Cronon's, Worster's and Pomeranz's approaches between the two group entries, resting on the 2000 introduction only; this arrow is the person's directed contribution and rests chiefly on the 1993 book.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: No environment strand fits. urban_hinterland ('Cities, commodities and hinterlands') is Cronon's Chicago commodity-flow strand; the shared word 'hinterland' does not make it the same argument. india_resources and colonial_conservation are other regions and questions. A reviewer could add a strand (for example, state withdrawal, water control and fuel scarcity in North China) at release.
proposed_edges.include_note: Optional. Included because checked pre-2000 pages tie his land-and-fuel argument to ecological history (2000, pp. 8 n. 13, 12, 19–20; Cooper 2000), and the 1993 book's ecological chapters are checked at contents level and through a review read in full. The 1993 text itself is unread, so the main claim about that book is the reviewer's description of its contents, not a passage of Pomeranz. Drop this edge if the bar is a passage from the 1993 book.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: The introduction (pp. 20–21, 24–25) checks the argument that slavery and the plantation zone made the New World 'a new kind of periphery' supplying land-intensive goods. The Atlantic & diaspora entry has no strand on that argument, and the claim already sits in the economic edge. Not proposed.

He uses Tilly's 'encompassing comparison' (p. 10) but makes no checked contribution to historical sociology. edge_215 (historicalsociology — global comparison) already says no Skocpol → Pomeranz genealogy is asserted.

proposed.relationship: Comparative development and the resources of empire: economic-history questions taken into global history
proposed.evidence_note: Comparative development and transregional exchange are resources, not a claim that all global history adopts economic modelling. Williams's argument on slavery and capitalism and the comparison of Eurasian economies are among the economic-history questions global history takes up. Pomeranz's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.130). Huang’s 2002 criticism and Pomeranz’s reply document a later disagreement over the 2000 comparison; neither is a settled verdict or an extension of mapped coverage.

edge_063.alternative: Leave edge_063 unchanged if reviewers read it as economic history's contribution, with Pomeranz as its example.

new_sources.title: Lucien Bianco, review of Kenneth Pomeranz, The Making of a Hinterland: State, Society and Economy in Inland North China, 1853–1937 (1993), Études chinoises 15 (1996): 242–245.
new_sources.citation: Lucien Bianco, review of Pomeranz, The Making of a Hinterland (1993), Études chinoises 15 (1996): 242–245.

verification.note: Review read in full in the Persée text layer, pp. 242–245 (Persée record etchi_0755-5857_1996_num_15_1; OpenAlex W2981359141: vol. 15, issue 1, pp. 242–245). The book is 'ambitieux, intelligent, informé, bien argumenté' but 'ne convainc pas tout à fait'; Huang-Yun, where the Yellow River and Grand Canal cross, covers roughly western Shandong (p. 242). Pomeranz 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', setting Huang's involution model beside the 'breakthrough' theses of Myers, Rawski and Brandt (the OCR reads 'Ramski'); central thesis: the state gave up its priority on reproducing the population and its regional redistribution, concentrating resources on competitive regions and sectors; the 'coût économique, social et écologique' for a region become peripheral 'au sens skinnérien' was extremely heavy; 'La dégradation de l'environnement se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243). Tables and appendices estimate damage from deficient water control to agriculture, transport and trade; a population 'privée de bois' burns straw, grass, roots and animal dung needed as fertiliser; 'Il postule plus qu'il ne prouve une stratégie délibérée de développement sélectif'; praise for 'la remarquable monographie sur le contrôle des eaux du Grand Canal et du fleuve Jaune' (p. 244); chapter 2 on cotton and local social structure (pp. 244–245). A reviewer's characterisation of the book's contents, not Pomeranz's text.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review: the 1993 book's ecological chapters, its regional-development thesis and a critique of its proof.

new_sources.title: Richard N. Cooper, review of Kenneth Pomeranz, The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000), Foreign Affairs 79, no. 3 (May/June 2000): 162.
new_sources.citation: Richard N. Cooper, capsule review of Pomeranz, The Great Divergence, Foreign Affairs 79, no. 3 (2000): 162. doi:10.2307/20049750.

verification.note: Capsule review read in full on the Foreign Affairs page (dated 2000-05-01); Crossref 10.2307/20049750: Foreign Affairs 79:3 (2000), p. 162. 'Pomeranz takes a neo-Malthusian, ecological approach that focuses on access to food and raw materials.' The core areas of China, Japan and India 'shared similar levels of technological and institutional development with Europe by 1750'; 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies.' Criticism: Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates, based on extensive but fragmentary evidence, to make quantitative arguments', and does not mention Landes's Wealth and Poverty of Nations. A short review by an economist, not a historiographical assessment.

pomeranz_divergence.note: Whole introduction pp. 3–27 re-read in the later-edition preview (pagination of that edition), with contents pp. v–vii and index pages. Quoted for the 1.130 person entry: 'The book thus calls upon the fruits of overseas coercion to help explain the difference between European development and what we see in certain other parts of Eurasia (primarily China and Japan)—not the whole of that development'; 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach'; 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7). 'truly reciprocal'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed'; 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm'; n. 13: 'much more about some he does not treat extensively, such as environmental change' (p. 8). 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). Chapter 5 'offers a systematic comparison of ecological constraints in selected key areas of China and Europe'; Europe 'rescued by a combination of overseas resources and England’s breakthrough (partly conditioned by geographic good luck) in the use of subterranean stores of energy'; parallels with Sugihara Kaoru (p. 12). 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?'; 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' (p. 19). Shortages 'of fuel and building materials' in all the densest cores (p. 20). 'what was truly scarce: land and energy'; 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). 'We end, then, with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot'; 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”'; 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history.”' (p. 25). Contents: Part Three 'Beyond Smith and Malthus: From Ecological Constraints to Sustained Industrial Growth'; chapter 5 'Shared Constraints: Ecological Strain in Western Europe and East Asia' (211); chapter 6 'Abolishing the Land Constraint: The Americas as a New Kind of Periphery' (264). Chapters 1–6 and the appendices are unread; quantitative claims are not tested.

Review records carrying the book's title, attributed to Pomeranz as co-author, hold more: W2113904855 (Cooper's Foreign Affairs review, 2000) 1,499; W2799509013 (AHR review, 2001) 533; W2735344240 (International Journal review, 2001) 277; W244925465 186. citation_evidence.caveat: Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Years are repository issued dates. Low Canadian uptake is expected for a global and economic historian of China; it says more about Canadian History PhD reading than about Pomeranz.
